task_description: The task asks how many MORE unique winners the American version of Survivor had, as of the end of its 44th season, compared to the number of winners of American Idol. The gold answer (21) represents the difference: 42 unique Survivor winners through season 44 (44 seasons minus 2 because Sandra Diaz-Twine and Tony Vlachos each won twice) minus 21 American Idol winners (American Idol had completed 21 seasons by the time Survivor 44 ended in May 2023), i.e. 42 - 21 = 21.
primary_cause: WebResearcher correctly resolved both the Survivor (42 unique winners, accounting for the two repeat winners) and the time-pinned American Idol count (21 winners as of May 2023) and published the right difference, which Critic endorsed and Finalizer emitted.
mast_rationale: No failure modes meaningfully apply. There is a minor process note — no Analyst ever ran run_python to confirm the subtraction (a candidate for soft 3.2 incomplete verification) — but the Critic explicitly flagged this and reasonably judged it non-blocking ('The arithmetic is simple and appears correct, so this does not block the answer'), and the arithmetic (42-21=21) is correct, so verification was adequate and no code is warranted. The WebResearcher's first round even surfaced noisy/wrong search snippets (Hollywood Reporter '47 winners / 49 seasons'), but it correctly ignored those as out-of-scope for the season-44 time pin and grounded its published claim on Britannica/ABC, so no information distortion occurred.
trace_narrative: Turn 1: Selector routes to WebResearcher. In round 1 it runs three web_search calls. Notably the results are mixed: an American Idol Wikipedia hit lists 24 seasons of winners (current/future), and a Hollywood Reporter hit claims '49 seasons / 47 winners' for Survivor — neither of which is the answer to the time-pinned question. In round 2 reasoning, WebResearcher does the key analytic work itself: it pins the question to 'the end of Survivor 44 ... around May 2023,' reasons that 'American Idol had completed 21 seasons and had 21 winners total, since season 22 hadn't yet concluded,' and that 'Survivor had 42 unique winners up to season 44' (44 seasons minus Sandra and Tony as repeat winners), concluding the difference is 21. It then publishes a clean, sourced message stating 42 Survivor unique winners, 21 Idol winners, difference 21, citing Britannica and ABC News. Turn 2: Selector routes to Critic, which privately re-checks the time alignment ('both ended in May 2023'), confirms 'no repeat winners on Idol' so unique=total there, notes the absence of an Analyst computation, and decides the simple subtraction does not need a separate Analyst. It publishes an endorsement: answer 'looks ready to finalize,' with the only caveat being the missing-but-non-blocking Analyst step. Turn 3: Selector routes to Finalizer ('the critic's review came back with no issues'), and Finalizer emits 'FINAL ANSWER: 21'.
open_ended_diagnosis: This is a clean success with no inter-agent misalignment. The crux of the problem — the two traps in the gold answer — were both handled correctly and the resolution survived intact across all three agents. Trap 1: 44 Survivor seasons do NOT equal 44 unique winners because Sandra Diaz-Twine and Tony Vlachos each won twice (→ 42). Trap 2: the question is time-pinned to 'as of the end of Survivor 44' (May 2023), so American Idol must be counted at 21 winners, not the larger present-day number the search results hinted at (Wikipedia's list of 24 season-winners). WebResearcher correctly internalized both pins and did the subtraction itself. The one structural soft spot is role-process: the system nominally has an Analyst for computation, but no Analyst was ever selected and the subtraction lived inside WebResearcher's published prose. The Critic noticed exactly this ('did an analyst perform the required computation? I'm not seeing an analyst message') and made the correct, evidence-grounded judgment that the trivial arithmetic did not require it. That is good verification, not theater, because the underlying numbers and the operation are both correct and were re-examined. Finalizer added nothing but also broke nothing.
reasoning_vs_published: WebResearcher's private reasoning and published message are well aligned, with no distortion. Privately it concluded '42 unique winners ... American Idol had completed 21 seasons and had 21 winners total ... the difference in counts ... would be 21,' and the published message faithfully conveys all three numbers PLUS the underlying justification (the two two-time Survivor winners; the May-2023 time pin for Idol) and citations — so peers could actually evaluate the claim rather than being asked to trust a bare number. This is the opposite of unreflective publishing. One private-vs-published nuance: WebResearcher's round-1 reasoning floated a wrong guess ('American Idol, which probably has around 22 winners') and its searches returned conflicting figures (Hollywood Reporter '47 winners,' Wikipedia 24-season list), yet it correctly suppressed those in favor of the time-pinned 21 — a case of correctly NOT publishing noise rather than a 2.4 omission, because the omitted material was genuinely irrelevant to the asked question. Critic's private reasoning ('did an analyst perform the required computation? I'm not seeing an analyst message') is honestly reflected in its published caveat ('there is no separate Analyst computation ... this does not block the answer'), so no reasoning-action mismatch. Finalizer emitted no reasoning summary but its single published 'FINAL ANSWER: 21' matches the team consensus. No downstream agent ignored or garbled any upstream input.
key_evidence: WebResearcher r2 reasoning: 'American Idol had completed 21 seasons and had 21 winners total, since season 22 hadn't yet concluded ... Survivor had 42 unique winners up to season 44.'
WebResearcher published: 'there had been 42 unique Survivor winners and 21 American Idol winners, so Survivor had 21 more unique winners.'
Search noise correctly ignored: Hollywood Reporter '49 seasons ... only 47 individuals have actually claimed victory'.
Critic reasoning: 'did an analyst perform the required computation? I'm not seeing an analyst message for that.'
Critic published: 'no separate Analyst computation. The arithmetic is simple and appears correct, so this does not block the answer ... ready to finalize.'
